opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing MIT gave me was a different relationship with being stuck. In math, you spend most of your time not knowing the answer. You stare at a problem for days, sometimes weeks, and nothing works. At MIT that was simply normal. Everyone around you was stuck on something, and nobody treated it as a sign that you didn't belong. It was just what doing hard things felt like.

There's a phrase people use, that getting an education at MIT is like drinking from a fire hose. At first that's overwhelming. You come in having been one of the strongest students wherever you were, and suddenly you're surrounded by people who are brilliant in ways you hadn't imagined. You can't keep up with everything. So you learn to prioritize, to accept that you'll fail at some things, and to keep going anyway. That humility was very important for me.

The culture is also very hands-on. "Mens et manus," mind and hand. Even in pure math, there was an attitude of "let's just try it." Compute small cases, write some code, test the conjecture, break it, try again. That instinct to act rather than wait for perfect clarity has stayed with me. It's a big part of why I was willing to leave a more traditional academic path and start building something. When you're doing a startup, especially at the frontier of AI and mathematics, you're stuck all the time. The difference is that now being stuck doesn't scare me. It feels familiar.

And there's the community. Late nights in the problem set rooms, people working through things together, sharing half-formed ideas without embarrassment. Perseverance is much easier when it's collective. You see your friends struggle and recover, and you realize resilience isn't some innate trait. It's something you practice, and the environment makes a big difference.

So if I had to sum it up: MIT taught me that difficulty is not a verdict on you. It's just the terrain. Your job is to keep walking.

r001.rationale: The response says that seeing MIT peers struggle and recover helped Carina realize resilience is practiced, and that perseverance is easier when it is collective. This clearly describes peers’ perseverance shaping her character by example.

fable-5.1.text:
I think MIT taught me that being stuck is the normal state, not the exception. When I arrived, I was coming from a world where I'd been used to things coming relatively easily, and then suddenly I'm in a problem set that's supposed to take ten hours and I've spent twenty hours on it and I'm still on problem two. Everyone around me was in the same situation. That's the thing about the culture there. It's not that people are suffering alone, it's that struggling is almost communal, almost celebrated. You'd walk into a lounge at two in the morning and there'd be eight people at a whiteboard arguing about something, and nobody thought that was strange.

What that did for me, I think, is it changed my relationship with failure. Before MIT, if I couldn't do something, I would read that as information about my ability. After MIT, I started reading it as information about the problem, like, okay, this is just hard, so what's the next thing I try. That's a small shift in framing but it changes everything downstream. It made me much more willing to attempt things where I had no idea if they would work.

The other part is that the people there genuinely cared about getting to the bottom of things. There was very little tolerance for hand-waving. If you said something was true, someone would ask you why, and you'd better have an answer or be honest that you didn't. I found that really freeing, actually, because it meant you were allowed to say "I don't know" without it being a weakness. It was just the starting point of the conversation.

So when I think about my character now, the perseverance isn't really about grinding harder. It's more about being comfortable in the uncomfortable state of not having an answer yet, and trusting that if you keep pushing at it honestly, something will give. I'm not sure I would have learned that anywhere else, at least not in the same intense, compressed way.

r001.rationale: The response describes peers working through difficult problems together and says this communal culture changed how Carina viewed failure and perseverance, showing how their example shaped her character.

astra-6.text:
I think it helped me become more comfortable with being stuck. When you’re surrounded by people who are tackling difficult problems, you realize that struggling doesn’t necessarily mean you’re doing something wrong. It can be part of the process of learning something new.

For me, perseverance isn’t just pushing harder at the same approach. It’s being willing to step back, ask for help, and try a different way. I think that’s the attitude MIT helped cultivate in me: taking the work seriously without treating every setback as a judgment of my ability.

r001.rationale: The response says that being around people tackling difficult problems helped shape Carina’s attitude toward struggle, but it does not identify the peers’ perseverance as a contagious example.
